subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Halo Effect
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Halo Effect usable.

hook.text: Attractive defendants get lighter sentences. Good looks signal nothing about guilt, yet juries are swayed.

buildup.text: The halo effect: one positive trait (beauty, fame, confidence) colors judgment of unrelated traits.

discovery.text: Edward Thorndike first documented it in 1920: military officers rated soldiers as good at everything or bad at everything.

twist.text: It works in reverse too. One negative trait—a lisp, a stain—can make everything about a person seem worse.

climax.text: Brands exploit halos: Apple's design reputation creates a halo that covers its pricing and restrictions.

punchline.text: One trait shouldn't color the whole picture. But it does.

quiz.question: What is the halo effect?
options: One positive trait biases judgment of unrelated traits

details.summary: The halo effect causes a positive impression in one area to influence judgments in unrelated areas. An attractive person is assumed to be intelligent and kind. A company with one good product is assumed to make all good products. First impressions radiate outward, coloring everything.
details.whyItMatters: The halo effect distorts hiring, grading, product reviews, and legal judgments. It shows how a single salient trait can overwhelm objective evaluation across all dimensions.
takeaways: One positive trait biases perception of all other traits
Physical attractiveness is the most studied halo trigger
The effect operates automatically and below awareness

faq.question: Who discovered the halo effect?
faq.answer: Edward Thorndike identified and named the halo effect in 1920 after studying military officer evaluations. He noticed that ratings on one trait like physique were highly correlated with ratings on unrelated traits like intelligence, suggesting a general impression was contaminating all judgments.

faq.question: How does the halo effect influence hiring decisions?
faq.answer: Interviewers who form a positive first impression tend to rate candidates higher on all dimensions including unrelated competencies. Attractive, confident, or well-spoken candidates benefit disproportionately. Structured interviews with standardized criteria help reduce the effect.
